text: This, My Friend climbs 900 feet of sustained crack and face climbing on excellent granite up the East Face of Dragontail's NE Towers. Established ground-up and onsight in August 2020 by Andy and Katherine Wyatt, Chris Potts, and Margot Fahey. Long pitches (up to 55m) with comfortable belay ledges and no fixed anchors; the route sits in the sun from early morning until early afternoon. Overall crux is 5.10a; individual pitch grades run 5.9+, 5.9, 5.6, 5.7, 5.7 from bottom to top.

text: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction with Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A at 2.6 miles, then continue to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3-4.4 miles and about 2,200 ft of gain. From the lake's south side, pick up the Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and ascend roughly 85% of the pass's height to about 7,250 ft (roughly 1,700 ft above the lake, most of the way up the pass's total ~2,200 ft), where the main trail crosses a large braided creek - the pass's primary water source, though it can thin out by late summer. Continue 5-10 minutes past this crossing, then leave the established trail between 7,300-7,400 ft and pick a rising traverse rightward across loose, unstable scree to the base of the route, about 300 ft below where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail. This off-trail scree section is the crux hazard of the approach - loose, exposed underfoot, and consequential given the terrain below.

text: From the top, traverse south and west across broken 3rd/4th class terrain, losing elevation gradually until reaching a clean gully roughly 500 ft below the final belay. Descend the gully to a large ledge, then scramble southwest to walkable ground where you intersect the standard summit descent trail down to Aasgard Pass; follow the cairned, braided climbers' trail down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) back to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls and watching for the common error of drifting climbers' right into cliffed terrain near Colchuck Peak. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer for the Aasgard Pass snow. This is a walk-off descent - the route is not set up for rappel.

text:
The base sits about 300 ft below the point where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail — so you are aiming under the junction of pass and mountain, not at it. Overshooting up the pass and then coming down is the common error.

The start is described as being in the middle of the protruding tower. On the ground the marker is above your head rather than at your feet: the first belay ledge is roughly 190 ft up and carries two bushes, and the route starts directly below the right-hand side of the right bush.

The first pitch also identifies itself by how it climbs. Fifty feet of easy ground leads to about ten feet of face moves around the right side of a recessed pod, and then back into the main crack system. If your first fifty feet is hard, or if there is no recessed pod to skirt, you are not on it.

The scree traverse in is the crux hazard of the approach — loose, exposed, and consequential given what is below.

edits.new: at which Aasgard Pass tops out against the foot of Dragontail

text: Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.

text: Past the gap, cross to the north side of the ridge and drop off-trail onto the top of the Queest-Alb Glacier. Cross it with axe and crampons, minding the moat between ice and rock and any open crevasses, then scramble rock and snow on the far side to the foot of the summit block. Three stacked ladders pinned into the rock climb the final band to the lookout; the move from the second to the third is the awkward one.

text:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the moat between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the south peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

text: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail except at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.

text: Two real options, and most parties take the walk-off. Option 1 (walk-off): from the East Shoulder, make an exposed, somewhat sketchy 4th-class traverse west (it borders on unprotected 5th-class slab in spots, so many parties stay roped) to gain the same descent gully used off the East Face. Downclimb the gully, then traverse north (right) to pick up the climbers'/cattle trail that runs up to Liberty Bell, which drops you onto the Blue Lake Trail; a faint climbers' path cuts off a final stretch of trail before the highway. Option 2 (rappel the route): from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 feet above the old P6 slung-block anchor. With double 70m ropes (a 70m lead line plus a 70m tag line) you can rappel from the very top of the route; doubled 60m ropes will not reach that first station. If you're bailing from above the P5 crux rather than finishing the route, two 60m ropes are workable using a fixed nut-and-sling anchor partway down P6 as an intermediate station — anything shorter risks coming up short between anchors. Lower down, the rappel stations are obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts. Hardware is mixed vintage: some original 1989 5/16" bolts remain despite a post-2016 rebolting push, and at least one older fixed-nut/sling anchor is noted as aging — back up or inspect any anchor you didn't place yourself before weighting it.

text: No source publishes a rappel total for this route, and the count moves with where you start, so no per-station distances are listed. The rope requirement is published and it is not a preference: the top station is a bolted anchor roughly 20-30 ft above the old pitch-6 slung-block anchor, and from it two 70m ropes reach the bolted anchor atop pitch 5 while doubled 60m ropes do not. A 70m lead rope plus a 70m tagline is the stated ideal because it keeps the option of rappelling from the very top; a party on doubled 60s has to break the first rappel at a fixed nut-and-sling anchor about halfway down pitch 6. Most parties do not rappel this at all — they top out on the East Shoulder and take the walk-off, a very exposed and sketchy 4th-class traverse west into the descent gully, which most keep the rope on for despite poor protection.

text:
Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft on the forest road system, reached either from Conconully to the south or from Winthrop to the southwest by the East Chewuch road. Both are long gravel drives of an hour or more; a third, gentler line comes over Baldy Pass on the South Fork.

From the campground, walk trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, roughly forty-five minutes of easy trail. Leave the trail there and traverse south across open grassy slopes into the small cirque at the base of the north face, about 7,360 ft.

The face rises around six hundred and fifty feet above the cirque and is split by couloirs and a rock tower. The whole approach is short and easy by the standards of this corner of the state, which is the point of coming here.

text: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail #1068 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain to the lake basin. Traverse around the west side of the lake over talus and boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system (snow-covered into early summer) toward the base of the North Peak's North Face. The standard North Face Route is a long, moderate alpine rock climb (Grade III, 5.6-5.7) on featured but sometimes rotten rock with significant brush; parties typically climb it car-to-car in a very long day (12-15+ hours) or with a bivy.

text:
US-2 at milepost 35.2, south on Mount Index Road 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the lake basin; the maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

Traverse the west side of the lake over talus and very large boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system toward the base of North Peak's north face. That gully carries snow into early summer.

Budget headlamps in the morning to reach the lake so the technical section starts at first light: parties commonly need 12 to 15 hours or more, and many bivy.

text: The trailhead is an unsigned climbers' and fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the Middle Fork road, roughly 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek trailhead at about 1,350 ft — no sign, no formal parking, and easy to drive straight past. Climb Green Ridge steeply, staying left where a fork drops northeast to Green Ridge Lake, over the ridge high point near 4,840 ft, past a small tarn, then down about 800 ft into the Upper Garfield lake basin and north through steep forest to Charlie Brown Lake. That mid-route descent has to be re-climbed on the way out, so it costs far more than the raw mileage suggests.

text: Charlie Brown Lake at about 4,390 ft is where the walking stops and the scramble begins, and it is the right place to stop because the whole remaining route is visible from its shore. From the outlet, work onto the peak's southeast slopes and thread up through broken cliff bands and duff to a broad talus field at roughly 4,850 ft — that talus field is the marker that you are on the correct line rather than one of the several plausible-looking weaknesses below it. From the top of the talus, angle left into an obvious gully with grassy slopes at its head. The gully is walled by rock on both sides and tops out near 5,400 ft at a notch beside a protruding rock on the south ridge, and it shoots you straight out onto the more south-facing slopes of the mountain. If you are traversing across the face rather than gaining height in a defined gully, you have gone past it. Above the notch the last few hundred feet are easy but steep heather to the summit ridge. Carry an axe and traction if snow is still sitting in that gully.

edits.old: it shoots you straight out onto the more south-facing slopes of the mountain
edits.new: it delivers you directly onto the mountain's more south-facing slopes

text: Start at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount) and park in the large lot above the boat ramp on the campground's south side — this is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead. Follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south about 6.5-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp (~1,900 ft), a backcountry stock camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek. The trail's original bridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties now cross on logs a short way upstream of the old bridge site. Across the creek, pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and around downed timber up the north ridge; a viewpoint near 4,600 ft gives the first look at Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Continue through forest and heather to Borealis Lake (base camp), a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle — it has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs — navigating crevasses to Lucky Pass, the Primus-Tricouni col. From Lucky Pass, climb a steep snow finger roughly 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then transition to rock ramps and ledges (class 3-4 scrambling) up the west ridge to the bouldery 8,102 ft summit. Hazards: crevasses on the Borealis Glacier (worse late season), a brushy and poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp, and afternoon softening of the snow finger.

edits.old: it has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs
edits.new: it has shrunk a great deal and now forms upper and lower tiers with slabs and cliffs between them

text: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (Sunrise Mine Trail #707) off the Mountain Loop Highway near Big Four/Barlow Pass. The trail begins in second-growth forest and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish via a log crossing that can be a genuine obstacle during high runoff (early season/after rain). From there the trail climbs steadily through Wirtz Basin, breaks out of the trees into open talus and boulder fields marked by cairns, and reaches Headlee Pass at roughly 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles in — a narrow, rocky notch/couloir with loose rock underfoot where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, then crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, which it follows up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead) — the last reliable running water before the climb. From the lake, cross the outlet and follow the summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then swing north across the slabs to the saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak. From the saddle, a ledge system cuts across Vesper's north face at roughly 5,800 ft, reached by walking out steep, exposed heather benches that get slick when wet and hold a steep snow slope into early-to-mid summer (ice axe and possibly crampons recommended for that window). The ledge leads to a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier remnant, near where True Grit's start is found. Allow 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route.

edits.new: starts in second-growth forest and, almost at once, crosses

text: Start from the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway at the pass, beside the ski area's substation and utility building, on the gated service road. Around a mile in, an easy-to-miss cairn-marked left fork leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge — staying right on the road takes you to a cell tower instead. Past the lake the route crosses the low point in Skyline Ridge, drops into a creek drainage on the ridge's back side, and climbs back out to gain the Tye Ridge crest. There is no maintained trail; snow-free this is a stiff bushwhack, which is why most ascents are made on continuous snow.

text: The route's crux is at its start, and the start goes down rather than up. From Skyline Lake climb northwest through timber to the low point in the crest of Skyline Ridge at about 5,200 ft. The far side is not a walk-through: it is a drop of roughly 150 feet at close to fifty degrees, mossy loose rock and brush when snow-free and liable to cornice in winter. That drop-in is the confirmation you are in the right gap — a gap you can simply stroll over is the wrong one, and there are several plausible low points along that crest. It bottoms out at the head of a small creek near 4,800 ft, an early-season water source and the last one. From there a steep wooded slope opens into gentle meadows around 4,900 ft and thins through timber to the crest of Tye Ridge near 5,000 ft, which is where the brush finally clears and the going turns to open heather benches. Follow the crest north to the saddle between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, then climb the ridgeline directly, staying on the highest ground to avoid cornices in winter and loose talus in summer.

text: Ultramega OK climbs the Northeast Buttress of Burgundy Spire — the hardest and least-traveled of the peak's four documented lines (5.11a, Grade III, 8 pitches, ~900 ft). From Burgundy Col, downclimb/scramble loose rock or steep snow around the north side of the spire to a twin-crack system marked by some obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up. The crux comes on P4, a thin corner leading into a roof at 5.11a; upper pitches traverse chimneys and cracks, with P8 finishing up an offwidth crack to the summit.

text: From Burgundy Col, descend around the north face to a twin-crack system with obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up (Action Potential's start is roughly 15 ft to the left). Eight pitches climb twin cracks, a chimney/right-facing corner, delicate face moves, and a bulging, thin-corner roof-traverse crux (P4, 5.11a) before wide cracks and chimneys and a final hand-crack/offwidth pitch reach the summit. Described by climbers as a good route that would be excellent with more traffic; some sections (notably the P6 corner) were noted as lichen-covered/dirty as of a 2018 ascent.

text: From the Smithbrook Road trailhead, hike the Smithbrook Trail roughly 0.9 mile up through old-growth forest to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near Union Gap. Leave the trail after a short distance and bushwhack northeast to gain Union Peak's southeast ridge at about 5,200 ft, then follow the ridge to the 5,696-5,700 ft summit. The line is an easy-to-moderate, non-technical alpine scramble in summer/fall and a moderate winter scramble or backcountry ski/snowshoe objective the rest of the year.

text: The Castle is a spire north of the main Dikes climbing area, with two bolted climbs to its top. Rock quality is poor and the approach is a bushwhack/scramble, but the exposure and summit view are notable.

text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on The Castle: from the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, continue about 1.2 miles further down the road (0.6 miles past where The Castle first becomes visible on the ridge) and park on the right (east) side where a dirt road from the Spangler Creek valley intersects the main road. Climb a long, very steep hillside to the base of the pinnacle.

text: Single rack to #1 with a few duplicates in the finger sizes. Recommended: 2–3 nuts in fingers, 2–3 mid-hand nuts, 2–3 hand-sized cams, 1–2 #1 cams. Small to medium nuts and slings optional but not required. 15 draws (mix of singles and doubles) recommended; 6 of these can be single runners.

text: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then up a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, then approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.

text:
Start at the Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish). Walk the pleasant, level main Barclay Creek trail for about 20 minutes and roughly a mile to a bridge crossing a large creek — often dry by mid-to-late summer.

Do not cross the bridge. Just before it, break right into the forest around a large boulder. Bushwhack through relatively open forest, or walk the creek bed, until you reach an open boulder field. Cross the boulder field to large trees and an open wash.

The wash leads to a steep, chossy, dirty waterfall; climb around its right side, staying out of the bushes — this stretch is exposed. Above that a ramp with hand lines, then a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, including a low-fifth step in a gully protected by a fixed line, and a small rock face with a bolt. Then roughly 800 ft of mostly roped slab in 35-50 m pitches on bolts and natural gear. Competent parties with good beta take two and a half to four hours; the approach is technical and hard to get right even with information.

text: The end of the fixed and roped section is where you unrope and scramble up and left to the base of the tower. The test the first-ascent party wrote down is a negative one and it is the most useful thing on this approach: if what you are doing feels sketchy, you are off the line. The approach is unpleasant but it is protected the whole way — fixed lines, hand lines, bolts — so unprotected, committing ground means you have lost the route, not that the route has got harder. The base of the tower is the foot of a nearly 1,500 ft overhanging prow; there is no mistaking it once you are under it.

text: Ares Tower is the highest of several named granite spires — Charon Tower, The Acropolis, Ares Tower, Vasiliki Tower, the Juno-Jupiter Towers, Aphrodite Tower, and Baccus Tower — strung along Vasiliki Ridge, which radiates north from the Wine Spires/Silver Star Mountain massif above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey and Herb Staley made the first ascent of the ridge on May 31, 1952; Beckey named it after Vasiliki Dwyer, a woman he met at Stevens Pass — the only Cascades feature he ever named after a woman. Despite its imposing look from the highway, Ares Tower itself is a moderate objective: essentially a 4th-class scramble to a notch just north of the true summit, finished by a short low-5th-class step (or an alternate direct low-5th variation up the west face).

edits.new: Beckey gave it the name of Vasiliki Dwyer, whom he had met at Stevens Pass

text: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles, then turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and follow it about 2.3-2.5 miles to its end at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass is required to park.

text: From the pullout head south and southeast toward the foot of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch, below the north side of Kangaroo Temple. Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. Around 5,800 ft you reach the level where snowpack commonly lingers well into summer.

text: Park at the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), about 1 mile east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 5,160 ft elevation). There's no formal trailhead sign or numbered trail here — the route to Kangaroo Pass is an unmaintained but well-cairned climbers' path on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land along the edge of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. From the pullout, head south/southeast toward the base of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch (below the north side of Kangaroo Temple). Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus field and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder/talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the approach, especially if snow-covered early in the season. The tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail once you're in the upper basin. Continue up mixed talus, boulders, and open slope to Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft), gaining about 1,500 ft over roughly 1.5 miles — typically 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water source on the approach and can be dry by late summer or fall; there is none higher, so carry enough from the car. Expect lingering snow from about 5,800 ft up to the pass into early-mid summer, depending on the year — an ice axe and/or microspikes are worth carrying into July. At Kangaroo Pass, leave the boot path and turn northeast onto Wallaby Peak's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail continues briefly then disappears on rock; stay on or near the ridge crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree, and grassy benches. At about 7,400 ft, swing around onto the south flank into the south-facing summit gully. This gully is moderately steep with notable loose rock and scree — wear a helmet, especially with more than one person in the party, since climbers above can kick debris down onto those below; some parties pick a short Class 3 line on the gully's margins to avoid the worst of the scree. Near the top of the gully, exit left (northeast) for the short final scramble to the true summit. Total distance is about 3.0 miles one-way (6.0 mi / ~2,900 ft round trip, or 9.7 km); budget roughly 1 to 1.5 hours car-to-pass and another hour pass-to-summit.

text: A striking twin-summit massif in the eastern Olympics, rising immediately north of Mount Constance (its nearest higher neighbor, 0.8 mi south-southeast) within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Warrior is the 11th-highest peak in the Olympic Range, built of Eocene-era pillow basalt uplifted with the range's obducted oceanic crust. Fred Beckey made the first ascent solo in 1945, climbing both the northwest and southeast (true, higher) summits in one push and naming the mountain; he's said to have carved his name into a rock at the saddle between the two summits, which some later parties report still finding.

text: This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. The route involves approximately 9-10 miles of approach hiking, making it a typical 2-day backpacking objective. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.

text: Drive Highway 101 to Sequim Bay State Park area, turn left on Louella Road for 1 mile, then left on Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles (it becomes FS Road 28 at the Forest Boundary), then turn right onto FS Road 2880, drive past Dungeness Forks Campground for 1 mile, stay left onto FS Road 2870 for 8.7 miles to Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Upper Dungeness Trail is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike the trail 3.4 miles and 600 feet to Camp Handy, then take the left fork and continue 3 miles and 1,850 feet to Boulder Camp (total: 6.4 miles, 2,450 feet gain). From Boulder Camp, continue south approximately 1.5-2 miles, crossing creeks, until you reach the final larger creek that flows from the cirque SE of Warrior Peak. Continue past this creek to a boulder field, then head up and back left toward the creek, staying under a band of cliffs, and continue up the boulders approximately 1 mile and 1,200 feet to reach the cirque at approximately 5,900 feet.

text:
The first test is a creek you must not cross. Leave the trail before crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb east — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — staying north of the streambed the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

The arrival test is the cirque at about 5,900 ft, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head north to the obvious couloir between the two peaks. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

The test at the top of the couloir is which way to turn, and it is the single most useful sentence for this peak in fog: at the saddle, the higher peak is on your right. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the right. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

Second test, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's northwest side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

What the season changes: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.

edits.new: forest first, then open meadow, then talus, all of it steep, and keep north of the streambed throughout
